I believe in the adaptation of our institutions to the government of all who will grow up within our limits. We have heard a great deal of sympathy for human liberty, sympathy for the human race. We have seen it producing evil falsely named good, and destroying instead of promoting the peace of the country. Suppose a portion of the people of any country have rebelled and you send troops there for the purpose of sustaining the weaker party against the stronger, do you not see that as soon as those troops are withdrawn the stronger party will recover their ascendency? Do you see that by your own principles the majority have the right to govern, and that when you send an army to force liberty upon people who do not understand it, when you have withdrawn that force, the stronger party will overpower and put down the weaker! The citizens of Santa Fe, in common with

proper regard for the interests of the territory

statement of facts to the attention of our fel-

On the 9th of March, 1537, Joseph Sarmi-
ento, Marquis de In Lagun, Viceroy of Mex-
ico, under the Government of Spain, issued a
decree, declaring the boundary between New
Mexico and New Biscay (now Chihuahua) to
be at the Rio Nombre de Dios, or Sacramento,
and described the village of El Paso to be with
the jurisdiction of New Mexico.


Don Juan Baptiste Pine, Deputy of the Prov.
ince of New Mexico, the Cortes of Spain, in
a memorial to that body, bearing date Cadiz,
1812, claims for New Mexico jurisdiction to
the 32nd degree of north latitude; and thus
the southern boundary of New Mexico seems
to have stood, until by an act of the Mexican
Congress, passed July 31, 1824, the northern
limits of the jurisdiction of the town called


El Paso were in the Province of Chihuahua, and necessarily
the southern boundary of New Mexico. In
the subsequent year, 1825, Chihuahua was, by
act of the Mexican Congress, erected into a
State, with the northern limits in the act of
1824. By no subsequent act of the
Mexican Government has this boundary line
been changed.


By the treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, the
boundary line of New Mexico, as laid
down in Disturnell's map, was made a part of
the boundary between the two Republics.


The southern boundary of New Mexico, as
laid down in Disturnell's map, strikes the Rio
Grande at a point not exceeding eight miles
above the town called Paso.


Tracing, then, all the changes in the posi-
tion of this boundary under the Mexican Gov-
ernment, up to the date of the treaty, it is
clear that New Mexico extended to the north-
ern limits of the town of El Paso, and that the
treaty so contemplated the boundary.


This territory, in dispute, was under the
jurisdiction of New Mexico, in a department
of Mexico. The civil authorities of the tem-
porary Territorial Government from 1846 to
1851, and the Territorial Government estab-
lished by the Congress of the United States,
continued to exercise jurisdiction over this
disputed territory until the illegal and unau-
thorized fixing of the initial point on the Rio
Grande, in 1851, at 32 deg. and 80 min. north
latitude, more than forty eight miles above the
town of El Paso, by Commissioner Bartlett.

of the Commissioners appear to the Gov-
ernment of the United States, that Congress
repudiated the act, and declared that the trea-
ty fixed the boundary not more than eight
miles north of El Paso. But this action of
Congress did not avert the immediate evils
following from the act of the Commissioner.
The Territory was immediately seized upon by
the Mexican authorities; American citizens
located there were despoiled of their property
and many Mexicans who had commenced the
settlement of Mexico, in 1847, with the under-

under the protection of the Government of
the United States, found themselves, against
their will, again under the Mexican Govern-
ment. Many of these citizens appealed to the
then Executive officer of this territory, but in
vain.

By this act, everything appears to have been left to Executive discretion, and no organization whatever prescribed by law.

On the 10th of July of the same year, however, an act was passed creating a single officer in this department called an accountant, whose duty it was made to account for moneys advanced and expended for the naval service.

Nothing further in the way of organization for the Navy Department was done until the passage of the act of the 8th February, 1816, entitled An act to alter and amend the several acts establishing the Navy Department, by adding thereto a board of commissioners. This act provided that the board of commissioners shall be attached to the office of the Secretary of the Navy and under his superintendence shall discharge all the ministerial duties of said office relative to the procurement of naval stores and materials and the construction, armament, equipment and employment of vessels of war as well as other matters connected with the naval establishment of the United States. The second section of this act also authorizes the commissioners to prepare such rules and regulations as shall be necessary for securing uniformity in the several classes of vessels, and their equipment, and for repairing and refitting them and for securing responsibility in the subordinate officers and agents."

Seventeen years after the establishment of the Navy Department, and twenty-six years after the establishment of the government, the first effort seems to have been made to secure responsibility in the subordinate officers and agents of the navy. The want of responsibility in the subordinate officers and agents is still the vice of the Navy Department. So far was the act of 1816 from effecting the desired object of securing responsibility, that it actually diminished, by dividing the little responsibility which before existed. The commissioners of the navy, by that act, were mere clerks to the Secretary of the Navy, to register his orders and employed principally in making contracts and collecting materials; and whatever information or advice they may have given on other and more important matters connected with the navy, was given without the obligation of law, and consequently without the public and serious responsibility which should attach to official advice.

Then, by the act of August 31, 1842, the act constituting the board of navy commissioners was repealed, and five bureaus were organized and attached to the Navy Department. These bureaus were:—

1. Bureau of Navy Yards and Docks.
2. Bureau of Construction, Equipment and Repair.
3. Bureau of Provisions and Clothing.
4. Bureau of Ordnance and Hydrography.
5. Bureau of Medicine and Surgery.

A CURIOUS LETTER.—The following is a
copy of a letter sent by a person in this city,
to President Pierce. It is curiosity in its
way:
Mr. President: I am well aware that there
are thousands of applicants for every Office
within your gift, out of which there are few
perhaps who are worthy or deserve to fill them,
yet all of them come with long petitions,
signed by many and respectable men. In my
case I can neither produce the one nor take
the other. Yet I feel I am capable of filling
the duties of any Office, and no less deserving.
I therefore address you to solicit the best of
your gift, and if you do not think it
worth your while to notice this you may be
sure that I shall work still harder for the glo-
rious cause of democracy, and shall, perhaps
have to see the day when Young Democracy
will triumph over Old Fogyism. Meantime
I hope to receive an answer to this with all
possible despatch, and allow me to subscribe
myself your friend but, rival for the presiden-
tial chair in 1856. Yours, respectfully.

ices within your gift, I shall be satisfied with
my old clothes you may have to give.

—Boston Times.

With this view, and for the purpose of establishing a system of responsibility and discipline throughout, it is recommended that the scientific corps on our side be placed under the immediate direction of Lieutenant Colonel Graham, to receive from him such written and verbal instructions as he may deem necessary to a full understanding of the duties to be performed in all parts of the work; and that all reports from the heads of parties be made to him, from time to time, as he may direct; and he will be required to report to you, as often as you may desire, all operations and their progress; and he will be held responsible to you for the successful prosecution of the scientific departments of the work. Should doubts arise between yourself and the Mexican commissioner, as to the proper location of any part or parts of the boundary described in the treaty, Lieutenant Colonel Graham will be required to cause to be surveyed any route, line or lines that you may deem necessary to elucidate and satisfy your mind in relation to any such questions, and make report to you thereon, accompanied by such plans or drawings as you may deem necessary. For the accuracy and faithful execution of these duties, he will be held responsible to you the commissioner of the United States.

Congress no doubt thought proper to allow this additional compensation in consideration of the laborious and responsible duties devolving upon that officer.

On reference to the law, it is found that the pay of Lieutenant Colonel Graham (he being paid &c. according to his rank as major of Topographical Engineers) is sixty dollars per month, seven hundred and twenty dollars per annum. He will, therefore, be entitled to receive from the appropriation for the running and marking this boundary line the sum of two thousand two hundred and eighty dollars per annum, and in that proportion from the time he may receive his orders from this Department; and he will be allowed ten cents per mile for his transportation while travelling on duty connected with the commission.

For these allowances he will be authorized to draw on this Department, payable in Washington, as he may prefer. His personal expenses will be allowed him in addition, as have been, or may be, allowed to other officers of the commission, due regard being had to his rank.

When the field duties shall be completed, or at any time that it may be found absolutely necessary to suspend them, owing to impediments of climate, etc., the plotting and drawing of the maps will be prosecuted under the direction of the head of the scientific corps, and under your general supervision, in cooperation with the Mexican commissioner and his scientific corps; the selection of the draughtsmen and the other members of the scientific corps on our side, to be approved by Lieutenant Colonel Graham and yourself, due regard being had to their scientific qualifications.

I am, sir, very respectfully, your obedient servant, ALEX. II. STUART,

BOSTON, April 9th, 1853.
W. L. GARRISON, Esq:

DEAR SIR,—Mr. Mann dislikes the length
of my letters. I am sorry they are so long,
both for his sake and that of your readers.
It might perhaps quote, in defence, the saying
Of the old English divine, Ignorance can
ask more questions in an hour than Wisdom
can answer in six months; but that might
be thought personal. The question, how
ever, is so comprehensive, that I cannot
promise to be very brief.

At last Mr. Mann enters upon frank and
elaborate defence of his conduct in the mat.
ter of colored schools. I am glad of it. It
is a duty which he has long owed to the
anti-slavery public, and to his own good
name. If any reader thinks his defence a
satisfactory one, MR. Mann should thank me
for this opportunity of making it; for I as
sure him, he has never had, among abolition

what he now claims. In my opinion, the
facts on which he rests his defence only
deepen his guilt. I never saw nor heard of
the articles in the Common School Journal to
which he refers. But have the most entire
confidence in his personal veracity, and if
he wishes to be understood to say that nine
years ago he opposed the separate education
of colored children, in articles published
with the full responsibility of his name, I
accept it as a fact. In view of it, I should
not again use the precise phrase did, that
he never gave us one word of recognition,
countenance or aid. But I should still assert
exactly the same in substance, namely
that he never gave us any substantial or
public assistance.

Bearing, however, this claim of his in
mind, let us examine his other statements.
The first is, what he did, twenty years ago,
as Trustee of the Institution for the Blind.
The meetings and records of those Trustees
are private. What could know, what could
the public know, of the opinions expressed
at those meetings, or recorded on those
books? All that the abolitionists, all that
the public knew, was that the only colored
child, who, about that time, applied for ad-
mission in the Institution, was refused. As
in other cases, we were obliged to judge the
Trustees by their public actions, which we
knew, not by their private opinions, which
we could not know.

took place in his parlor, or private rooms, at
Bridgewater. I could not know, and surely

a conference held in one, about that time,
in which his views as to the admission of

at all what he now represents them to have
been. MR. Mann does not suspect me of
this base trick attempted on him at Bridge-
water some eight or ten years ago, not ye-
t far from the time of one of my attacks
on him. This is very generous in him, see-
ing that my attacks were made five years and
three months ago, just three or four years after
the alleged trick! "You rolled the water
was drinking last spring," said the wolf to
the lamb. "But I was not born then," said
the lamb. Does Mr. Mann remember the

To the EDITOR of THE New-York Times

SIR—In the Crystal Palace among the thousands of articles on exhibition there is entitled New York Elevated Railroad and Promenade for the relief of Broadway, worthy indeed of especial notice and patronage, being the only tangible remedy for this great thoroughfare. The plan is got up in mastery style and modelled with great perfection in brass. There is also a block of houses either side of the elevated railroad modelled large scale in wood, showing at a glance the imposing effect of this truly desirable project, credit to the inventor. The people of New York are well acquainted with the many dreadful accidents daily occurring to life and limb from the overgrown state of traffic and travel in Broadway, besides the hindrance and detention to BOTH, calling immediately for protection and accommodation. Should private and interests of few be put forward to retard progress designed for the masses! For instance, who among the enlightened would be so poor philanthropist as to let life and limb suffer wholesale, lest property should deteriorate in Broadway! I feel satisfied none could descend to so mean conclusion. But instead of being lessened, it shall endeavor to prove it would be much enhanced. The second story could be converted into an light fancy BAZAAR worth about three times the present rent. The third story becomes second from the promenade and would nearly double in value; and so on proportionally to the top story. The great difficulty yet to be solved: Some PEOPLE imagine the elevated railroad would darken the first floor and consequently depreciate their value. This mistake arises from the hurried conclusion of those who are unacquainted with the merits of the proposed construction, intended to be built right over the street, feet from the grade. One half the entire surface would be glass panelling of both railroad and promenade. The reflection of light from this half would nearly equal thorough light. In short, the whole structure would do nothing less than brilliant DOME shading Broadway from the summer's sun and winter's storm. The sidewalk, on either side, is about 15 feet wide without any interruption of light whatever, being entirely open except where a platform may be required for the entrance of the second story stores, the fronts of which may be glass supported throughout by iron columns 2 feet apart, besides being open from one side to the other. Another objection goes to prove that when travel becomes transferred to the promenade, that business takes flight, not out of Broadway, but to the second story only. Retailers would move to the second story, making room for wholesale men. This would be the very thing to enrich Broadway. Merchants would lump at such central position and pay as high rents as are paid at present.

In fine, by the erection of this desirable railroad, life and limb would be preserved, thorough accommodation for the public, light sufficient for any business, and vast increase in property and business; and last not least, the panoramic beauty and splendor of Broadway, especially by night, would have no equal in the world.

New-York, Nov. 10, 1853.

SUICIDE BY ARSENIC.—Coroner Wilhelm yesterday held inquest at the house No. 161 Second St. upon the body of Ludwig Bselchle, German, 35 years of age, who committed suicide on Wednesday afternoon by administering to himself an overdose of arsenic which he had procured at the drug store of Mr. Mercke in Grand St., where he stated that he wanted it to kill rats. The deceased, a pedlar of very intemperate habits, for some time past had been almost constantly intoxicated. He had also had several attacks of delirium tremens. After taking the poison, he informed the inmates of the house, but his statement was not believed and medical aid procured until too late to save his life. A verdict of suicide was rendered by the Jury.

Fatal RAILROAD.—Coroner Gamble held an inquest yesterday at the New York Hospital upon the body of a German, about 10 years of age, whose name is supposed to be Alonzo Neak, who died from the effects of injuries received the 18th inst. by being run over by a train on the New Jersey Railroad. It appears that he was walking the track in the curve of the Bergen Hill, at the time the engineer, seeing him, sounded the alarm whistle and reversed the engine; the brakes were also put down, and the train had almost stopped when one wheel passed over his body. It is thought that he had ample time to get off the track. The Jury rendered a verdict of accidental death.

Fatal RAILROAD ACCIDENT.—On Wednesday evening, an Express train of the Hudson River Railroad from Albany, nearing the depot at Thirty-fourth St., ran over O'Neil, a flagman, who, standing on the track, was run down before the Engineer could stop the train and was instantly killed. His remains were taken to the depot, where Coroner Hilton yesterday held an inquest upon them. The evidence went to show that the death was accidental, and the Jury rendered a verdict to that effect. Deceased, native of Ireland, 50 years of age.

SUDDEN DEATH.—Coroner Gamble held an inquest YESTERDAY at the house No. 9 East Eleventh St., upon the body of Sarah Ford, who died suddenly on the evening previous. The evidence adduced went to show that the deceased had been very intemperate in her habits; post mortem examination revealed the fact that death was caused by congestion of the brain produced by intemperance, and the jury rendered a verdict to that effect. The deceased was in extremely destitute circumstances; her husband having left her some time since and gone to Pennsylvania, where he is said to have died. She leaves two small boys who were taken in charge by a relative living in Second St.

AGGRAVATED ASSAULT.—Messrs. John G. Simmonds and Jeremiah Riley, both engineers of the New York and New Haven Railroad, a short time since, while passing up Broadway near Canal, at about 11 o'clock at night, heard a cry of murder, and on looking about for the purpose of ascertaining whence the cry proceeded, approached two men, of whom they made inquiry relative to the alarm. Instead of giving them a suitable answer, the two men, who were John Arcularus and James Quinn, commenced a violent assault upon the gentlemen and knocked them down, beat, and kicked Mr. Simmonds in a most outrageous manner. Three of his front teeth were knocked out by a slug shot or some similar weapon, and his face was so much disfigured that the wounds are not yet healed. The back of his head was also severely cut. Mr. Riley was also attacked by the accused and severely beaten. Officer Martin of the Fifth Ward, hearing the disturbance, came up and arrested Quinn, who was locked up in the Station House for the night. The railroad meeting at Stanstead last Wednesday was numerously attended, and promises to yield valuable results. Several roads in New England were represented by their Presidents or Directors, while many other influential gentlemen not connected with railroads were also present. The Canada side was represented by some of the best men in the Provinces, among whom may be mentioned Attorney General Drummond, Mr. Papin, member of the City Council of Montreal, Col. Yeule and A. L. Allard, of Chambly, and numerous others. Great enthusiasm was manifested, especially by those living along the line of the proposed road from Stanstead to Montreal.

Hon. L. J. Terrill, N. P., presided over the meeting. T. T. Phillips, Esq. and J. K. Robinson, Esq., officiated as Secretaries. Numerous speeches were made by gentlemen from both sides of the Line, all of whom expressed great confidence in the success of the project and pledged their most vigorous effort to accomplish it as speedily as possible. Among the speakers were Gov. Fairbanks, Col. N. B. Baker, of N. H., Hon. Geo. W. Kittredge, of Newmarket, Hon. Geo. W. Nesmith, of Franklin, Hon. Josiah Quincy, of Rumney, and Mr. Huntington, of Shefford, Attorney General Drummond, of Quebec, Councillor Papin and Mr. Ostell of Montreal, Mr. Fay, of Boston, and Gen. Joseph Low, of Concord, N. H.

Many of the gentlemen from New Hampshire and Massachusetts had never seen Orleans County before, and all of them expressed their surprise and admiration, at seeing so beautiful and fertile a section of country. It was very apparent that railroad into that country would find an abundance to do. The grain, the cattle, the dairy products and the lumber would furnish an abundant supply of freight. Stanstead County also took all the strangers by surprise. The sun does not shine upon a more lovely landscape than that which greeted the eyes of those who assembled on the hill of Stanstead Plain. It was very apparent too that the land is as productive as it is beautiful. Unless we greatly misjudge, the effect of this meeting will be much greater than has been produced by any similar meeting in that part of the country. — Caledonian, 19th inst.

It is with great satisfaction, that in the exercise of the privilege allowed me, as the Chief Magistrate of the State, of addressing you on this occasion, and so near the close of my official term, I am able to congratulate you upon the auspicious circumstances under which you are assembled. The period is one of general and unparalleled prosperity, especially in all the material elements of improvement in the condition of the country. The earth has given forth its fruits in unwonted abundance; and if some of the great agricultural staples are likely to be diminished by the autumnal rains, all the more important and indispensable products of the soil, are plentifully distributed. Industry is stimulated by new enterprises. The artisan and the laborer find ready employment with increased and remunerating wages, and everywhere within our borders the comforts of life are being more equally and generally diffused. The facilities of intercommunication have been greatly increased. Our civil and religious institutions and privileges are extended to all classes of our people, and contribute greatly to their happiness and welfare. General good health has pervaded our land, and it becomes us to acknowledge, with grateful hearts, our obligations to an all wise and beneficent Creator for the blessings he has bountifully bestowed upon us. But in congratulating you upon the general prosperity and happiness, I am pained to be compelled to state that there has been some drawback. Though we have abundant cause to be grateful for the blessings of general health, yet within some localities of limited extent in our own State, sore disease has brought mourning into the dwellings of many worthy families; while our sympathies have been deeply moved by the destroying pestilence with which an all wise Providence has thought proper to afflict our brethren and countrymen in the great Commercial Metropolis of the South, and of many other cities and towns upon the Gulf and over Mississippi. HOT CORN! Here's your nice Hot Corn,
smoking hot, smoking hot, just from the
pot" Hour after hour, last evening as we
sat over the desk, this cry came up in a soft,
pitiful voice under our window, which told
us of one of the ways of the poor to excute
the means of subsistence in this overburdened,
loud and worse-lodged home of misery
--of so many without means, who are con-
stantly crowding into the dirtiest purlieus of
this vigorously dirty City, where they are
exposed to the daily chance of death from
some sudden outbreaking epidemic like that
now desolating the same kind of streets in N.
Orleans and swallowing up its thousands of
victims from the same class of poverty--stricken,
uncomfortably provided for human beings
who know not how, or have not the power to
flee to the healthy hills and green fields of the
country. Here they live--barely live--in
streets almost as hot as the hot corn, the cry
which rung in our ears from dark until
midnight.
"Hot corn, hot corn here's your nice hot
corn," rose up in faint child-like voice
which seemed to have been aroused by the
sound of our step as we were about on the
Park, while the City Hall clock told the
hour when ghosts go forth upon their mid-
night rambles. We started, as though sin-
ister hands had given us a rap, for the sound seemed
to come out of one of the iron posts which
act as sentinels over the main entrance
forbidding all vehicles to enter, unless the
driver takes the trouble to pull up and turn
out of the way of one of the aforesaid posts,
which is not often done, because one of them,
often, if not always, is out of its place, giving
free ingress to the courtyard, or livery
stable grounds of the City Hall, which is
of the growth of few miserable
and dusty brown trees and doubtful grassy
patches, we call "the Park."

Looking over the post we discovered the
owner of the hot corn cry, in the person of
an emaciated little girl about twelve years
old, whose dirty frock was nearly the color of
the rusty iron, and whose face, hands and
feet, naturally white and delicate, were grimed
with dirt until nearly of the same color.
There were two white streaks running down
from the soft blue eyes, that told of the hot,
scalding tears that were coursing their way
over that naturally beautiful face.

"Some corn, Sir," lisped the little suffer-
ing girl, caring to speak to one who did not
address her in rough tones of command such
as "give me some corn, you little vagabond," or name still more opprobrious both
to herself and mother. Seeing we had no
look of contempt for her, she said, piteously,
"please buy some corn, sir."

"No my dear, we do not wish any; it is
not very healthy in such warm weather as
this, and especially so late at night."

"No dear, then, what shall I do?"

"Why, go home. It is past midnight, and
such little girls as you ought not to be in the
streets of this bad City at this time of night."

"I can't go home--and am so tired and
sleepy. Oh dear."

"Cannot go home. Why not?"

"Oh, Sir, my mother will whip me if I go
home without selling all my corn. Oh, sir,
go buy one ear, and then I shall have only
two left, and am sure she might let little Sis
and me eat them, for I have not had anything
to eat since morning, only one apple the man
gave me, and one part of it he threw away. I
could have stole a turnip at the corner, but
then I went to get sometime in a pitcher for mother, but dare not take, she

A L'ASSEMBLÉE
A l'Ordinaire Président et Messieurs les Ministres du Conseil des Assistants de la Ville de la Nouvelle-Orléans

Messieurs—J'ai été requis de transmettre votre Honorable Corps la pétition ci-incluse signée par un grand nombre de citoyens reconnus, demandant que les instruments planétaires de Barlow actuellement en exhibition à l'Institut des Artisans, soient achetés par le Conseil Commun, pour l'usage des Écoles Publiques de cette ville.

En appuyant cette accommodation, que j'approuve de tout cœur, je ferai observer que l'inventeur de ces instruments remarquables, a réussi à placer sous les yeux le mouvement entier du système solaire, tel qu'il luit, jour par jour et année par année, et indiquer d'une manière fort compréhensible la position relative de la Terre et de la Lune et des planètes inférieures, à toute époque passée, présente ou future. Des instruments aussi parfaits et aussi uniques doivent, dans mon opinion, aider beaucoup à développer chez les enfants la science astronomique et lui donner un certain attrait, parce que les mouvements des astres sont exécutés de manière à être compris de tous.

En conséquence, j'aime croire que votre Honorable Corps voudra bien rendre ce mémoire en considération, et nommer un comité qui s'occupera de savoir si ce tableau planétaire peut être utile aux Écoles Publiques.

Je suis, respectueusement,

Votre obéissant serviteur,
